passage: The festival's submission portal closed at midnight, the flat's internet kept dropping, and Uday's short film about his grandfather's tailoring shop was still sitting on his laptop. For an hour he had been refreshing the group chat, waiting for Akash and the others to say it was good enough. Two had reacted with a thumbs-up. Nobody said 'send it'. At 11:20 he closed the chat. He wrote on a sticky note: Would I be proud of this if nobody clapped? Under it he listed what he cared about: honest, slow, Nanu's hands. He watched the film one last time, just for himself. Yes. The pride was quiet, but it was there. He still wanted people to love it; that didn't go away. But it wasn't driving anymore. At 11:54, with one bar of signal, he pressed submit. Then he texted Akash: 'Sent. Watch it when you can.'

qa.q: What was Uday's short film about?
qa.a: It was about his grandfather's tailoring shop.

qa.q: How did Uday feel after watching the film just for himself?
qa.a: He felt a quiet pride based on his own values, even though he still wished others would love it.

qa.q: What did Uday do that loosened the grip of approval?
qa.a: He stopped waiting on the group chat, asked whether he'd be proud without applause, and listed his own values before deciding to submit.

qa.q: How might Akash feel getting 'Sent. Watch it when you can'?
qa.a: Akash might feel pleased and a little surprised that Uday submitted without waiting for everyone's verdict.

grounding: Racing a deadline, an adult asks whether his film would make him proud even if nobody clapped, and submits on his own values.

passage: At the family lunch in their Vadodara flat, Nirmala Maasi asked the question everyone was thinking. 'You turned down the bank job? For an NGO?' Alka felt the old heat rise in her face. For years she had chosen whatever made the aunties nod. Last night, before telling anyone, she had written in her diary: Would I be proud of this choice if nobody said well done? And under it, her own reasons: teaching girls in the basti, work that feels true, enough to live on. She had read it twice, and the answer was yes. Now she took a breath. 'Yes, Maasi. It's what I value.' Nirmala Maasi shook her head and changed the subject. It stung. Alka still wished she'd said shabaash. But she ate her lunch without the sick feeling she used to get, and on the bus home she felt steady.

qa.q: Which job did Alka turn down?
qa.a: She turned down the bank job.

qa.q: How did Alka feel when Nirmala Maasi disapproved?
qa.a: It stung and she still wished for praise, but she felt steady rather than sick, because her choice rested on her own values.

qa.q: What did Alka do before telling her family that helped?
qa.a: She wrote whether she'd be proud without anyone's praise and listed her own reasons, so the choice rested on her values rather than on reactions.

qa.q: Why might Nirmala Maasi shake her head?
qa.a: She may worry about Alka's security and future, seeing the bank job as the safe, respectable choice.

grounding: A young woman checks whether her career choice would make her proud without praise, and stays steady when family disapproves.

passage:
'Do you think people will like it?' Dilnaz held up the invitation for her first small exhibition.
Imran looked at the painting on the card: the old women selling fish at the Mahim market. 'Do you?'
'I asked first.'
'And I'm asking you. If nobody came, if nobody said a word, would you be proud of these?'
Dilnaz opened her mouth, then closed it. 'That's not fair.'
'Why not?'
'Because I want them to like it.'
'Of course. So do I. But that's the second question.'
She looked at the card for a long time. 'Yes,' she said finally. 'I'd be proud. They're honest. I spent two years at that market.'
'Then that's your answer. The rest is extra.'
'Extra would be nice, though.'
Imran laughed. 'Extra would be very nice.'
That night Dilnaz wrote on the back of her sketchbook: Honest. Two years. Proud. She stuck it above her easel.

qa.q: What does the painting on the invitation show?
qa.a: It shows the old women selling fish at the Mahim market.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel after answering 'Yes, I'd be proud'?
qa.a: She felt a steady pride in her honest work, while still honestly wishing people would like it.

qa.q: Why was writing 'Honest. Two years. Proud.' above the easel useful?
qa.a: It keeps her own values in view before any reactions arrive, so approval has less grip on how she feels.

qa.q: Why does Imran answer her question with a question?
qa.a: Imran wants Dilnaz to find her own approval first, so others' opinions become 'extra' rather than the main thing.

grounding: An artist is asked whether she would be proud of her work if nobody came, and sets her own values ahead of others' reactions.

passage: Last Sunday I did long division for one whole hour. Twenty sums, and they kept going wrong at the last step. When I finally finished, my head felt like cotton wool. I went to the kitchen and ate the whole packet of biscuits Mummy was saving for guests. Then my brother Pradeep asked to borrow my pencil, and I shouted at him to go away, which wasn't fair, because it was his pencil. Mummy found me sulking on the balcony. She said, 'Vinita, after a big hard job, brains often get cranky and hungry. Grown-up scientists still argue about exactly why. But it happens.' I said sorry to Pradeep. Now, after hard homework, I go on the swing for ten minutes before anything else.

qa.q: How many sums did Vinita do?
qa.a: Vinita did twenty sums.

qa.q: Why did Vinita shout at Pradeep over a pencil?
qa.a: Vinita felt tired and cranky after an hour of difficult sums, which left less patience than usual.

qa.q: What new habit did Vinita start, and why might it help?
qa.a: Going on the swing for ten minutes after hard homework gives a rest before dealing with snacks or people.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel being shouted at over his own pencil?
qa.a: Pradeep would likely feel confused and a bit hurt, since he only asked to borrow it.

grounding: A child remembers finding it harder to resist biscuits and keep her temper after an hour of hard sums, while the reason is still debated.

passage:
Tuition centre note, Thursday.
Today Mahima did a full hour of fraction practice for Saturday's test, the longest she has managed. She worked hard, frowning, and got most of them right. Straight after, the change was clear: she ate three packets of chips from the snack shelf in five minutes, then argued with Nakul about whose turn it was on the computer and pushed his chair. This isn't like her. I think after that much effort her patience simply ran low. Researchers still debate why this happens, and it may not be a simple 'running out' of willpower. Whatever the reason, the pattern was obvious today. I spoke with her calmly, she apologised to Nakul, and I told her mother at pickup. Plan: break the hour into two halves with a ten-minute outdoor break, and move snacks to before the session.
Harsha

qa.q: How many packets of chips did Mahima eat?
qa.a: She ate three packets in five minutes.

qa.q: Why did Mahima push Nakul's chair?
qa.a: After an hour of hard fractions she felt tired and her patience ran low, so a small disagreement felt much bigger.

qa.q: What changes does the tutor plan?
qa.a: Splitting the hour into two halves with a ten-minute outdoor break, and moving snacks to before the session.

qa.q: How might Nakul feel when Mahima pushes his chair?
qa.a: Nakul would likely feel surprised and upset, since this isn't how Mahima usually behaves.

grounding: A tutor's note shows a child losing patience and self-control after an hour of hard maths, while noting the cause is debated.

passage:

I did the algebra worksheet for a whole hour tonight, the hard one with brackets. By the end my brain felt fizzy and empty at the same time. Then I ate four of Abbu's chocolates, even though I'd promised to save them. Then Yash called to ask about the science project and I snapped at him for calling during dinner, which wasn't even true; it was after dinner.

Abbu said that when brains work hard for a long time, people often get snappy and snacky. He said scientists argue about the exact reason, so nobody knows for sure, but he always feels it after long meetings too.
Tomorrow I'm going to do the worksheet before lunch, when I'm fresh, and nowhere near the chocolate tin.
Zeenat

passage: Home in Kumbakonam for the holidays, Lakshmi, a second-year psychology student, watched her cousin Disha drop onto the veranda after a long day at the tailoring shop. 'Don't ask me to study for my typing test,' Disha said. 'My willpower is finished. I read it on my phone: it's like petrol, it runs out.' Lakshmi smiled. Two weeks ago her professor had spent a whole lecture on exactly that idea. 'It was a famous theory,' she said. 'But when big teams repeated those experiments with thousands of people, most couldn't find the effect.' Disha frowned. 'So I'm not tired?' 'You're definitely tired. That part's real. It's just that nobody's sure it's a tank. Some studies even suggest that believing it runs out makes people give up sooner.' Disha thought about it. 'So what do I do?' 'Maybe rest first, then try fifteen minutes. See what happens.'

qa.q: What did Disha say willpower is like?
qa.a: She said it's like petrol and runs out.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi feel about the petrol idea, given what she has learned?
qa.a: Lakshmi feels doubtful about it but careful, respecting Disha's real tiredness while being unsure the tank explanation is right.

qa.q: What balanced suggestion does Lakshmi make?
qa.a: Rest first, then try fifteen minutes and see what happens, since tiredness is real but the mechanism is uncertain.

qa.q: How might Disha feel hearing 'You're definitely tired'?
qa.a: Disha would likely feel understood and relieved, not accused of being lazy.

grounding: A psychology student at home explains that large replications did not confirm willpower as fuel, while treating her cousin's tiredness as real.

passage: In the university library in Oslo, Ingrid was halfway through her essay on self-control when she hit the paper that changed it. She had started out sure of her argument: willpower is a fuel tank; use it and it empties. Every textbook summary said so. But the article in front of her described a huge replication, dozens of labs, thousands of participants, and the strong effect had mostly vanished. Another study suggested that people's beliefs about willpower changed how drained they felt. She leaned over to Zanele. 'Did you know the fuel-tank thing might not be true?' Zanele shrugged. 'I still feel wrecked after exams.' 'That's real,' Ingrid said. 'Nobody's saying tiredness isn't real. It's the explanation that's shaky.' She deleted her first paragraph and started again: 'Evidence on self-control fatigue is mixed.' It felt less satisfying and more honest.

qa.q: Where was Ingrid writing her essay?
qa.a: She was writing it in the university library in Oslo.

qa.q: How did Ingrid feel deleting her first paragraph?
qa.a: She felt a little less satisfied but more honest, having come to doubt a neat theory once the evidence turned out mixed.

qa.q: How did Ingrid change her essay to fit the evidence?
qa.a: She began with 'Evidence on self-control fatigue is mixed', keeping tiredness real while showing that the mechanism is uncertain.

qa.q: How does Zanele experience the debate?
qa.a: Zanele cares more about feeling wrecked after exams than about the theory, and Ingrid agrees that tiredness is real.

grounding: A psychology student discovers that large replications failed to confirm strong depletion effects and rewrites her essay to reflect the uncertainty.

passage: By seven, Nirmala had made what felt like a thousand decisions: which candidates to shortlist, which of two angry managers to call back first, whether to approve a leave request. Then the rain turned the ride home through Pune into a ninety-minute crawl. When she finally dropped onto the sofa, the gym bag she'd promised herself looked like a mountain. 'Just order biryani,' she said aloud, and did. Her flatmate Gautam came in to find her eating from the box. 'Gym?' 'Can't. No energy left. My brain's done choosing.' 'Is it energy, or are you bored of it, or does it just matter less at night?' Nirmala thought. 'All three, maybe.' 'Then try mornings,' Gautam said. 'And pack your gym bag the night before, shoes on top.' Nirmala sighed. The next evening she laid out her kit before bed. At 6:30 the next morning, half asleep, she went.

qa.q: How long was the ride home?
qa.a: It was a ninety-minute crawl.

qa.q: Why did the gym bag look like a mountain to Nirmala?
qa.a: After a day of decisions and a long, rainy commute, she felt drained and bored, so even small choices felt too heavy.

qa.q: What changes helped Nirmala?
qa.a: Moving workouts to the morning, so the hard thing comes first, and packing the gym bag the night before to lower friction.

qa.q: How does Gautam see Nirmala's tiredness?
qa.a: Gautam takes it seriously but wonders whether it's energy, boredom or priorities, and focuses on practical fixes.

grounding: After a day of decisions and a rainy commute, an adult orders food and skips the gym; doing the hard thing earlier and preparing ahead helps.

passage: At the end of every shift at the café in Indiranagar, Pradeep had made hundreds of small choices: which table got the corner seat, whether to comp the cold coffee, who could leave early, how many croissants for tomorrow. By ten at night, walking into his one-room flat, he had nothing left. He ordered a pizza on his phone, again, and let his guitar sit in the corner, again. He'd told himself he would practise every night. It had been three weeks. On Sunday his colleague Harish, who cooked in the café kitchen, said, 'Why don't you practise before your shift? And eat what we make here, instead of deciding at ten.' Pradeep laughed, then thought about it. On Monday he played for twenty minutes at noon, before work, and took a box of the staff dal home. By ten he was tired, but there was nothing left to decide.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep keep ordering pizza at ten at night?

qa.q: How might Harish see Pradeep's routine?

grounding: A café manager drained by a day of choices orders takeaway and skips guitar, until doing it earlier and removing evening decisions helps.

passage:
'You said you'd run tonight,' Seema said, as Imran collapsed onto the sofa with a takeaway menu.
'I know. I can't. I made about four hundred decisions today.'
'Four hundred?'
'Budgets, vendors, which intern gets which project. My brain's a wet towel.'
'Or you're bored of running.'
Imran paused. 'That too, maybe.'
'Or it just feels less important at nine than it did at seven this morning.'
'Are you a scientist now?'
'I read that nobody's sure why evenings are like this. Tired, bored, different priorities. Maybe all of it.' She took the menu away. 'But whatever it is, it keeps winning at nine.'
'So?'
'So run at seven in the morning. Leave your shoes by the door tonight. I'll come with you on Wednesdays.'
Imran groaned. Then he got up and put his shoes by the door, laces already loosened.

passage: With his sister's newborn in the flat and the whole family taking turns walking her at night, Harish's evenings had become useless for his thesis. For weeks he sat down at nine, stared at the screen, and called himself lazy. His brother Bhupen, rocking the baby, said, 'You're not lazy. You're writing at the worst hour of your day.' So Harish tried something else. He noticed he was sharpest between six and eight in the morning, before anyone woke. He moved his writing there. In the evenings, instead of fighting himself, he did easy things: laid out his clothes, packed his lunch, wrote tomorrow's first sentence on a sticky note. Within a month the chapter that had been stuck since spring was drafted. The baby still cried at night. Harish slept through some of it now, and he stopped calling himself lazy.

qa.q: When was Harish sharpest?
qa.a: He was sharpest between six and eight in the morning.

qa.q: How had Harish felt about himself during the stuck weeks?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and ashamed, calling himself lazy for failing to write at nine at night.

qa.q: How did Harish plan around his energy?
qa.a: He wrote at his sharpest time, six to eight in the morning, and used evenings for easy preparation like clothes, lunch and tomorrow's first sentence.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see his brother's struggle?
qa.a: Bhupen sees it as a timing problem, not laziness, and says so kindly while rocking the baby.

grounding: In a noisy house with a newborn, an adult moves his hardest work to his best hours and prepares evenings ahead, instead of blaming his character.

passage: Tejas had been trying to prepare for job interviews after work, and every evening in their Hyderabad flat ended the same way: laptop open, brain blank, phone in hand, then guilt. 'I'm just undisciplined,' he told his sister Sarita on Sunday. Sarita, who ran a clinic's front desk and planned everything, handed him a notebook. 'When do you feel sharpest?' He thought. 'Before work. Seven to eight-thirty. The office is quiet till ten.' 'Then that's interview time. Evenings are for the easy stuff.' They spent Sunday afternoon cooking five boxes of rajma-rice for the week and choosing his office clothes. On Monday Tejas did ninety minutes of practice problems at seven, before anyone else came in. In the evening he just ate, laid out his clothes, and went to bed. By Friday he had done more than in the whole previous month, and the word 'undisciplined' had quietly disappeared.

qa.q: When is Tejas sharpest?
qa.a: He is sharpest before work, from seven to eight-thirty.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel about himself before the change?
qa.a: He felt guilty and blamed himself as undisciplined after every blank evening.

qa.q: What did Tejas and Sarita change?
qa.a: They moved interview practice to his sharpest morning hours, and cooked meals and chose clothes on Sunday to reduce evening choices.

qa.q: How does Sarita see Tejas's problem?
qa.a: Sarita sees it as a scheduling issue, not a flaw in his character, and responds with a plan.

grounding: An adult moves his most important preparation to his sharpest hour and prepares meals and clothes ahead, instead of calling himself undisciplined.

passage:
'You've blocked ten to twelve every day?' Dolma peered at Saurabh's calendar. 'No meetings?'
'That's when my brain works. I write the monthly report then.'
'And the rest of the day?'
'Calls, emails, the stuff that doesn't need my best thinking.'
'I used to think you were just more disciplined than me.'
Saurabh laughed. 'I'm not. At four I can't write a sentence. I used to force it and then call myself lazy.'
'What changed?'
'I stopped blaming myself and started noticing. Mornings good, afternoons foggy. So I stopped fighting it.'
'What about evenings?'
'I decide dinners on Sunday. Same three meals, rotating. I lay my clothes out at night. Fewer choices when I'm tired.'
Dolma looked at her own calendar, full of meetings from nine. 'I schedule my hardest work at five,' she said slowly.
'How's that going?'
'Terribly.'

qa.q: Which hours has Saurabh blocked every day?
qa.a: He has blocked ten to twelve every day.

qa.q: How did Saurabh use to feel when forcing himself to write at four?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and ashamed, calling himself lazy when the foggy afternoon made writing impossible.

qa.q: How does Saurabh plan around his energy?

passage: When Uday Mamu came to their flat in Bhopal, he always made promises. 'I'll take you to the zoo on Sunday.' 'Next time I'll bring the big kite.' Sunday came and went. The kite never came. So this time, when he held out one chocolate and said, 'Take this now, or wait till tomorrow and I'll bring you a whole box,' Afreen took the chocolate before he finished the sentence. Mamu laughed. 'No patience, this girl!' Afreen said nothing and ate it quickly. Later, her mother sat beside her. 'Why didn't you wait for the box?' Afreen shrugged. 'He never brings things.' Her mother was quiet for a moment. 'That's fair,' she said. 'It's not about patience, is it?'

qa.a: Keep small promises reliably, like actually bringing the kite, so that waiting starts to feel worthwhile.

qa.q: How does Afreen's mother see the choice?
qa.a: Her mother understands it as a sensible response to broken promises, not a lack of patience.

grounding: A child who has learned that her uncle breaks promises takes the reward at once, a reasonable choice rather than weak character.

grounding: A child who has seen her father's promises broken chooses a small toy now over a promised cycle, a reasonable choice when the future is unreliable.

passage: When I was younger, at my old school, Coach Ramesh used to promise things. 'Win the district match and everyone gets new shoes.' We won. No shoes. 'Practise all summer and we'll go to Pune for the tournament.' We practised. No Pune. So by the time I was nine, I had stopped waiting for anything grown-ups promised. At my new school, when the librarian said, 'Anand, you can borrow one book now, or reserve the new comic series and get all five next week,' I took one book straight away. My friend waited and got all five. I felt a bit stupid. But I also remembered the shoes. It took a whole term of the librarian keeping every promise before I trusted her enough to wait.

qa.q: What did Coach Ramesh promise for winning the district match?
qa.a: He promised new shoes for everyone.

qa.q: Why did Anand take one book straight away?
qa.a: After many broken promises, Anand didn't trust that waiting would pay off, so taking what was in front felt safer.

qa.q: What helped Anand learn to wait?
qa.a: A whole term of the librarian keeping every promise, which rebuilt trust that waiting would be rewarded.

qa.q: How might Coach Ramesh's broken promises have affected the other players?
qa.a: They likely felt let down too, learning, like Anand, that adults' promises might not come true.

grounding: A child looks back on grabbing rewards at once after a coach's broken promises, a sensible choice when the future felt unreliable.

passage: The night before her history test in Cape Town, Zanele knew what would happen if her phone stayed on the desk: one quick look at the game, then an hour gone. It had happened on Tuesday. So this time she muted the game's notifications, walked to the kitchen, and put the phone in the bread drawer. Her sister Valentina raised an eyebrow. 'Hiding from your own phone?' 'Yes,' Zanele said. 'I'm not strong enough to ignore it. So I'm not going to try.' Back in her room, the desk was just a desk: notes, a pencil, a glass of water. Twice she reached for the empty spot where the phone usually sat. By ten she had finished two chapters. She collected the phone from the bread drawer, played one round of the game, and went to bed.

qa.q: Where did Zanele put her phone?
qa.a: She put it in the bread drawer in the kitchen.

qa.q: Why did Zanele say 'I'm not strong enough to ignore it'?
qa.a: She felt realistic rather than ashamed, knowing from Tuesday that willpower alone wouldn't beat the game, and was determined to study anyway.

qa.q: Why did putting the phone in another room work better than gritting her teeth?
qa.a: It removed the temptation from her space, so she didn't have to keep resisting, and she finished two chapters.

qa.q: How does Valentina react to the phone in the bread drawer?
qa.a: Valentina is amused and teasing, finding it funny that Zanele is hiding from her own phone.

grounding: A teenager mutes game notifications and puts her phone in another room before revising, changing her surroundings instead of gritting her teeth.

passage: At the boarding school hostel, evening study ran from seven to nine, and phones were allowed in rooms. For three weeks Vishal had kept his on the desk 'just in case', and for three weeks the racing game had eaten most of his study hours. On Monday he walked down to the warden's office at 6:55 and handed his phone over. 'You can keep it,' the warden said, surprised. 'I know,' Vishal said. 'I don't want to.' Back in the room, his roommate Omkar was already three races in, the sound up. Vishal put in earplugs and turned his chair to face the wall. His chemistry notes had never looked so interesting. By nine he had done both worksheets. When he collected his phone, he felt oddly proud, as if he'd outsmarted himself.

qa.q: What time did Vishal hand over his phone?
qa.a: He handed it over at 6:55.

qa.q: Why did Vishal feel 'oddly proud' collecting his phone?
qa.a: He felt determined and pleased that changing his surroundings, not sheer willpower, let him finish both worksheets.

qa.q: What changes did Vishal make to his environment?
qa.a: He handed the phone to the warden, put in earplugs, and turned his chair to face the wall, away from Omkar's game.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Vishal's new routine?
qa.a: Omkar might find it strange or funny, since phones are allowed in rooms and he is busy playing.

grounding: In a boarding hostel, a teenager hands his phone to the warden and blocks out a noisy game to study, changing his environment instead of relying on willpower.

passage:
Dear Chetan Bhai,
You asked how I finally got through board revision without the game eating my evenings. Honestly, I gave up trying to be strong.
For months I told myself, 'Just one match, then study.' One match became six. So in January I changed the room instead of changing me. I muted every game notification. I gave my phone to Ammi at seven every evening, and she put it in her cupboard. I moved my desk away from the doorway where I could see the TV. I kept only the book I needed on the table.
The first week I kept reaching for my pocket. By the third week I didn't even think about it. My maths went from 61 to 84 in the pre-boards.
So my tip: don't fight the phone. Put it somewhere you can't reach.
Rehana

qa.q: What did Rehana's maths score rise to in the pre-boards?
qa.a: It went from 61 to 84.

qa.q: What did Rehana mean by 'I gave up trying to be strong'?
qa.a: Rehana felt frustrated with willpower that kept failing and became realistic about it, so changing the room felt smarter than relying on strength.

qa.q: What changes did Rehana make to the study space?
qa.a: Muted game notifications, gave the phone to Ammi at seven, moved the desk away from the TV view, and kept only the needed book on the table.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel keeping the phone in her cupboard each evening?
qa.a: Ammi would likely feel glad to help and proud to see the maths score climb.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager explains beating a gaming habit by changing the study environment rather than relying on willpower.

passage: Mehak was twenty-one and in her first month as a trainee at a nursery in Bandra. Little Kavitha, four, could not wait for anything. If snack was in five minutes, she cried. If the swing was taken, she pushed. So Mehak started small. 'After this song, you get the swing. I promise.' Then she sang the whole song, with Kavitha counting the verses on her fingers, and when it ended, Mehak took her to the swing. Every time. When snack was late, they counted to twenty together, loud and silly. If Mehak said 'after lunch', it was after lunch, never later. By the end of the month Kavitha could wait through a whole song without crying, humming along. One day Mehak heard her tell another child, 'Wait, wait. Mehak Didi always comes.'

qa.q: What did Kavitha count on her fingers?
qa.a: She counted the verses of the song.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha say 'Mehak Didi always comes'?
qa.a: Kavitha had come to trust Mehak because every small promise was kept, so waiting no longer felt frightening.

qa.q: What did Mehak do that built Kavitha's ability to wait?
qa.a: She kept every small promise exactly and gave Kavitha a way to wait by singing and counting together.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel hearing Kavitha say that?
qa.a: Mehak would likely feel moved and proud that her reliability had taught Kavitha that waiting pays.

grounding: A young nursery trainee keeps small promises and teaches a child to wait by singing and counting, and the child learns waiting pays.

passage:
'I want the ice cream now!' Baljeet stamped his foot.
'After dinner,' Pallavi said. 'I promise.'
'You'll forget.'
'Did I forget the park on Saturday?'
Baljeet thought. 'No.'
'Did I forget the story last night?'
'No.'
'So, after dinner. Want to count the minutes with me?'
'That's too many.'
'Then let's sing the train song three times. That's dinner time.'
'Three times?'
'Choo choo, off we go. One.'
Baljeet sang, grumbling, then louder. By the third song, the dal was on the table. He ate fast. Then he looked at Pallavi.
'Ice cream,' she said, and opened the freezer. 'See? After dinner.'
Baljeet licked the spoon. 'Didi, you always remember.'
'Always,' said Pallavi. 'That's the deal.'

qa.q: What song did they sing while waiting?
qa.a: They sang the train song three times.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet say 'You'll forget'?
qa.a: He was impatient and worried the promise wouldn't be kept, so waiting felt risky.

qa.q: How did Pallavi help Baljeet wait?
qa.a: She reminded him of promises she had kept, like the park and the story, and gave him a way to wait by singing the train song.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when Baljeet says 'you always remember'?
qa.a: Pallavi would likely feel warm and proud that her reliability is teaching him that waiting pays.

grounding: An older sister caring for her little brother keeps her promises and helps him wait with a song, teaching that waiting pays.

passage: When I started coaching the under-tens at the colony ground last year, I made promises casually. 'Bowl well and you'll bat next.' Then time ran out and they didn't. I noticed Tanvir, eight, stopped waiting his turn. He'd grab the bat, sulk, walk off. At first I thought he was just impatient. Then I remembered: I'd broken my 'you'll bat next' three times with him. Why would he wait? So I changed. I only promised what I could keep. 'Three overs of fielding, then you bat.' And I kept it, every time, even when practice ran late. While they waited, we counted balls aloud or sang the silly boundary song. By March, Tanvir stood at the edge with his pads on, counting under his breath. 'Darshan Bhaiya, two more balls,' he'd say. He believed me.

qa.q: What did Darshan start promising instead?
qa.a: He started promising, 'Three overs of fielding, then you bat.'

qa.q: What did Darshan realise about Tanvir's impatience?
qa.a: Darshan felt a pang of guilt, realising Tanvir had no reason to wait after three broken promises.

qa.q: What changed Tanvir's ability to wait?
qa.a: Darshan kept every promise and made waiting fun by counting balls and singing, so Tanvir learned that waiting pays.

qa.q: How does Tanvir show his trust by March?
qa.a: He stands ready with pads on, counting balls under his breath, sure his turn will come.

grounding: A young cricket coach looks back on learning to keep small promises and make waiting fun, which taught a child that waiting pays.

passage: In their house in Nagaur, evenings used to go the same way for Devika: dinner, then the phone, then suddenly it was eleven and her maths book was still in her bag. Telling herself 'I'll study tonight' never worked. So on Sunday she wrote a sentence on the inside cover of her maths notebook: If dinner is over, then I open this book before I touch my phone. Her sister Sunaina read it and laughed. 'That's it? That's your big plan?' 'It's specific,' Devika said. On Monday, after dinner, her hand went to her pocket out of habit. Then she remembered the sentence. She put her plate in the sink, took out the notebook, and opened it. Once it was open, starting was easy. By Friday it happened almost without thinking. The phone still came out, just after twenty sums instead of before.

qa.q: Where did Devika write her sentence?
qa.a: She wrote it on the inside cover of her maths notebook.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when Sunaina laughed at the plan?
qa.a: She felt calm and confident, trusting that a specific plan would work better than vague promises.

qa.q: Why did the 'if dinner is over, then open the book' plan work?
qa.a: It linked a clear cue, the end of dinner, to one action, opening the book, so she didn't have to decide in the moment.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see the plan by Friday?
qa.a: Sunaina might be surprised it worked, seeing her sister open the maths book almost automatically.

grounding: A teenager writes an if-then plan to open her maths book after dinner before touching her phone, and the cue replaces in-the-moment choice.

passage: Esther's afternoons in Berlin had a problem: she got home at four, dropped her bag, and her thumbs found the game before her coat was off. By six, her German vocabulary list was untouched. Her brother Felix suggested willpower. That didn't work. Then her teacher mentioned something called an if-then plan. Esther wrote on a sticky note by the front door: If I take my shoes off, then I do ten vocabulary words before anything else. It sounded almost too simple. On Monday she took off her shoes, saw the note, and did the ten words standing in the hallway, bag still on her shoulder. It took eight minutes. After a week, taking off her shoes and reaching for the list had become one movement. Felix noticed. 'You haven't touched your phone at four all week.' 'I have,' Esther said. 'At ten past.'

qa.q: Where did Esther put the sticky note?
qa.a: She put it by the front door.

qa.q: How did Esther feel about the if-then plan at first?
qa.a: She felt doubtful, since it sounded almost too simple, but was willing to try after willpower failed.

qa.q: What made Esther's plan effective?
qa.a: It tied a specific cue, taking her shoes off, to a small action, ten vocabulary words, so the choice didn't rest on in-the-moment willpower.

qa.q: How does Felix see the change?
qa.a: Felix notices she is no longer on her phone at four and seems surprised by the difference.

grounding: A teenager ties a specific cue, taking off her shoes, to ten vocabulary words, so the plan replaces in-the-moment choice.

passage: At the residential school in Aligarh, the study bell rang at seven every evening. For Asif, it used to be the signal to check his phone 'one last time', which usually meant forty minutes of videos. His roommate Samir had read somewhere about if-then plans and dared him to try one. Asif wrote it on the first page of his physics notebook: If the study bell rings, then I open this notebook and solve one problem before anything else. On Tuesday the bell rang. His hand moved toward his phone, and then he saw the notebook lying on top of it, where he had left it on purpose. He opened it. One problem became four. By Friday, the bell and the notebook felt connected. Samir, who hadn't made any plan, was still watching videos at 7:40. Asif grinned and threw a pencil at him.

qa.q: What time did the study bell ring?
qa.a: It rang at seven every evening.

qa.q: How did Asif feel by Friday about the study bell?
qa.a: He felt steadier and more in control, since the bell had become a cue for the notebook rather than the phone.

qa.q: Why did putting the notebook on top of the phone help the if-then plan?
qa.a: It made the planned action the first thing he saw at the cue, so the right choice became automatic rather than a struggle.

qa.q: How might Samir feel watching Asif work while he watches videos?
qa.a: Samir might feel a bit sheepish, since he suggested the idea but hadn't tried it himself.

grounding: A teenager at a boarding school uses an if-then plan tied to the study bell to open his notebook before his phone.
